findings.category: OWASP A07 - Identification and Authentication Failures
findings.title: Google sign-in registers/logs-in any account with zero server-side verification
findings.description: registerWithGoogle() returns a valid JWT for ANY email if that user already exists. firebaseUid is accepted unvalidated and the Google ID token is never sent or verified server-side.
findings.exploit_scenario: 1. Attacker POSTs /api/auth/register-google with {"emailId":"victim@example.com","firebaseUid":"anything","userName":"x"}. 2. Server finds existing user, returns valid ADMIN JWT. 3. Attacker fully controls victim account.
findings.impact: Total account takeover for any registered user using only their email address.
findings.recommendation: Accept Google's ID token in the request and verify signature + audience server-side (tokeninfo or Firebase Admin verifyIdToken). Do not trust client-supplied firebaseUid/email.

findings.category: OWASP A07 - Identification and Authentication Failures
findings.title: Biometric login endpoint mints JWTs with no cryptographic proof
findings.description: POST /api/auth/biometric-login authenticates on userId + emailId only. Biometric verification happens entirely client-side; any caller who knows a victim's userId and email can mint a valid JWT. User IDs are sequential longs, so they are enumerable.
findings.exploit_scenario: 1. Enumerate userIds (1,2,3,...). 2. Obtain victim email (guess, prior data, or /api/auth/register-google response). 3. POST /api/auth/biometric-login {"userId":N,"emailId":victim} -> valid ADMIN JWT.
findings.impact: Account takeover; bypasses the only role gate (biometric) and feeds the /docs IDOR.
findings.recommendation: Require a server-verifiable proof (e.g., a short-lived signed challenge, or send the decrypted token and verify it) and bind issuance to that proof.

findings.title: Legacy /docs upload endpoints are missing shop-ownership checks (IDOR)
findings.description: All POST /docs/shops/{shopId}/<type>/upload endpoints are authenticated (anyRequest) but never call shopAccessService.validateShopAccess/validateShopOwner. PANDocumentService.uploadPAN and the 15 sibling services only call shopService.getShopById(shopId).
findings.exploit_scenario: 1. Any MANAGER (or any JWT via findings 1-2) calls POST /docs/shops/{otherShopId}/pan/upload with a file. 2. Server overwrites another shop's PAN document and S3 object.
findings.impact: Cross-tenant document corruption/overwrite; combined with finding 1-2, attacker can deface any shop's document store.
findings.recommendation: Add shopAccessService.validateShopAccess(user, shopId) in DocumentController for every upload endpoint, or migrate clients to the access-checked /api/shops/{shopId}/documents/{type}/reupload.

findings.category: OWASP A07 - Identification and Authentication Failures
findings.title: Manager 6-char access code is brute-forceable: no rate limit, no lockout
findings.description: login-by-code authenticates with a 6-char code from a 32-char alphabet (~1.07B combos). Public endpoint /api/auth/login-by-code has no rate limiting or account lockout. Codes are returned to admins and stored in plaintext (managers listing).
findings.exploit_scenario: 1. Attacker runs online brute force against POST /api/auth/login-by-code at high concurrency. 2. Eventually guesses a valid code. 3. Gets MANAGER JWT and access to assigned shops.
findings.impact: Account compromise of manager accounts; escalation via manager shops.
findings.recommendation: Add per-IP/per-code rate limiting, exponential lockout, and consider longer/high-entropy codes with expiry.

findings.title: S3 URLs returned as direct public-style URLs with fully predictable object keys
findings.description: uploadFile() returns https://{bucket}.s3.amazonaws.com/{key}. Keys are predictable (pan/shop_{id}/pan_card.pdf, msme/verify/{udyam}/udyam_certificate.pdf). The URL is returned in DocumentResponse (/api/shops/{id}/documents). If the bucket is public-read, all uploaded PII documents (PAN, FSSAI, licenses) are directly downloadable and enumerable; if private, the returned URLs are dead and the one-time-token design is the only working path.
findings.exploit_scenario: 1. Confirm bucket policy. 2. Enumerate https://{bucket}.s3.amazonaws.com/pan/shop_1/pan_card.pdf, shop_2, ... to harvest every uploaded PAN card.
findings.impact: Mass exposure of highly sensitive business PII if bucket is public; broken client URLs otherwise.
findings.recommendation: Enforce private bucket + IAM-only access, return presigned URLs (short TTL) or stream only via /api/documents/*, and use random object keys.

findings.title: Production Docker image runs as root on an unpinned mutable base image
findings.description: FROM mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:latest (mutable 'latest' tag, supply-chain risk) and USER root. No non-root USER directive, no pinned digest.
findings.exploit_scenario: 1. 'latest' tag is replaced by a malicious image, or app is compromised via RCE. 2. Attacker has root in the container, escalating to host-level compromise on weak isolation.
findings.impact: Full container compromise becomes host compromise.
findings.recommendation: Pin the base image to a digest or exact version, drop to a non-root user, use a distroless/JRE-only base, and remove Playwright if unused by the runtime.

findings.title: Android stores JWT in plaintext SharedPreferences with cloud backup enabled
findings.description: AuthResponse.token is written to MODE_PRIVATE SharedPreferences in plaintext (dukaan_api_prefs). AndroidManifest sets android:allowBackup=true with empty exclusion rules, so the plaintext JWT is eligible for ADB/cloud backup extraction.
findings.exploit_scenario: 1. Attacker with device access or a backup archive reads /data/data/<pkg>/shared_prefs/dukaan_api_prefs.xml. 2. Replays the JWT to fully impersonate the user.
findings.impact: Token theft leading to account takeover on device/backup compromise.
findings.recommendation: Move JWT to EncryptedSharedPreferences (or Android Keystore), set allowBackup=false or add exclude rules for the prefs files.

findings.title: Live Ola Maps API key committed and embedded in the APK
findings.description: OLA_MAPS_API_KEY=q01pyxLjrwKL33EYUaOB1M3uKLa0BI159T5KW9a4 committed to git, injected via BuildConfig into the APK and sent as a query parameter on every autocomplete call (AddBusinessScreen.kt:122).
findings.exploit_scenario: 1. Decompile the release APK (BuildConfig is plaintext) or sniff the autocomplete request. 2. Scrape the key and burn Ola Maps quota/charges, or use it from any IP.
findings.impact: Quota exhaustion, unexpected billing, key abuse from anywhere.
findings.recommendation: Revoke the key, move it to a backend proxy (the server already has OlaMapsConfig/OlaMapsRestClient), and serve results through your own API.

findings.title: H2 console and Swagger UI publicly exposed; default profile is dev
findings.description: /h2-console/**, /swagger-ui/**, /v3/api-docs are permitAll. application.properties defaults to SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=dev which enables the H2 web console (application-dev.properties:13). If prod is started without the env var set, the H2 console is network-reachable (RCE-capable via JDBC URL override/CREATE ALIAS) and the full API is documented publicly.
findings.exploit_scenario: 1. Prod instance accidentally starts with dev profile. 2. Attacker browses /h2-console, connects with sa/empty password, runs arbitrary SQL and gains JVM code execution.
findings.impact: Remote code execution in a misconfigured deployment; full API enumeration via Swagger.
findings.recommendation: Make prod the default profile, gate H2 console behind an env flag defaulting to off, and remove swagger/h2 from the permitAll list in prod.

findings.title: Android HTTP logging writes login passwords and JWTs to logcat in release builds
findings.description: HttpLoggingInterceptor.Level.BODY is set unconditionally (not gated by BuildConfig.DEBUG). Login request bodies (emailId+password) and AuthResponse (JWT) are logged in cleartext to logcat.
findings.exploit_scenario: 1. Attacker with adb logcat access (debug cable, rooted device, some cloud device farms) reads credentials and tokens.
findings.impact: Credential and token disclosure on any device where logs are accessible.
findings.recommendation: Gate logging behind BuildConfig.DEBUG and drop to Level.BASIC; never log auth payloads.

findings.title: Dev JWT secret and default DB password exist in git history
findings.description: dk-dev-default-secret-minimum-32-characters-long-for-hs256 (dev JWT secret) and a default Postgres password Dukaan@123 are present in git history (older configs). Current config requires env vars, but the values are burned into history forever and can be reused in any environment that sets a weak default.
findings.exploit_scenario: 1. Repo or history leak. 2. Attacker tries the known dev secret to forge JWTs against any instance running with that value.
findings.impact: Forged JWTs if any deployment uses the leaked default; informational for history hygiene.
findings.recommendation: Purge history with git filter-repo/BFG, rotate any credentials matching the leaked values, and ensure no deployment uses defaults.

findings.title: Local H2 database files committed to git
findings.description: server/data/fssai.mv.db and fssai.trace.db are tracked (commit f2a1bed). No PII strings found in current content (24KB, empty dev DB), but the file grows with use and must not be in the repo.
findings.exploit_scenario: Future commits leak live dev data (emails, mobiles, manager codes, hashes) via the DB file.
findings.impact: Potential future data leakage; repo bloat.
findings.recommendation: git rm --cached server/data/* and add server/data/ to .gitignore.
